production.title: Can We Still Trust What We See Online? Google Opens Its AI Reality Check

narration:
Three media types can now be checked,
but this tool can't tell you what's human.
Google opened SynthID Detector globally in English,
so upload an image, video, or audio file
and check SynthID, an invisible watermark
used by Google and partner tools.
At a busy market stall, that's like checking a seller's stamp
before trusting a dramatic clip on your phone.
Upload the clip, and it may say
“SynthID detected,” or highlight the marked section.
A positive result means Google or a partner system,
including OpenAI, NVIDIA, or Kakao, created or edited part of the file.
So it's evidence, not proof about every second,
and the same check can inspect an image, video, or recording.
There's a trade-off, though, because “not detected”
doesn't prove human-made; another system may have created it,
or heavy editing may have hidden the mark.
So pause before sharing, run the check,
and treat it as a clue, not a verdict.
If you want more clear evidence checks like this, follow the channel,
because the next breakdown picks up here.
And until then, a market stall stamp helps, but it isn't the whole story.

research.summary:
Verified G$LIDE explainer brief: “Google’s AI detector has a catch.”

Hook: Show a dramatic, suspicious-looking video. Upload it to SynthID Detector. The result appears: “SynthID detected” or “not detected.” Then explain the crucial limitation: this is a watermark check, not a universal test for whether something was made by a human.

Suggested 30-second script: “Google is opening SynthID Detector worldwide in English. It can scan an image, video or audio file for an invisible SynthID watermark—used by Google and participating partners to label some AI-generated content. A positive result is a strong signal that Google or a partner AI system created or edited at least part of the file. But a negative result does not prove the content is real: it may have been made by another AI tool, or the watermark may no longer be detectable after extensive edits. So before you share a shocking clip, treat the detector as one clue—not a final verdict.”

Visual sequence: 1) Freeze-frame on the suspicious clip. 2) Upload animation. 3) Highlight the detected segment or “no watermark detected” result. 4) Split-screen: “AI watermark found” versus “not proven human-made.” 5) End card: “Would you trust an AI detector before sharing a shocking video?”

Editorial note: Avoid calling SynthID a definitive “AI detector.” The strongest accurate framing is “a detector for SynthID watermarks from Google and participating partners.”

claims.claim: Google announced on October 7, 2026 that SynthID Detector would be available globally in English to everyone.
claims.source_title: Google expands SynthID Detector for AI content

claims.claim: The detector can check image, video and audio files for SynthID watermarks.
claims.source_title: Google expands SynthID Detector for AI content

claims.claim: Google says SynthID Detector can identify content made with Google AI or participating partner tools, including OpenAI, NVIDIA and Kakao; Apple is described as coming soon.
claims.source_title: Google expands SynthID Detector for AI content

claims.claim: A detected SynthID watermark indicates that all or part of the media was created or edited by a compatible Google or partner AI system; it does not establish that the entire file was generated by AI.
claims.source_title: Verify AI-generated images, videos and audio

claims.claim: A result showing no SynthID watermark does not prove that a file was made by a human, because it may have been created by another AI system or may not contain a detectable watermark.
claims.source_title: Verify AI-generated images, videos and audio

claims.claim: Google says SynthID watermarks are designed to remain detectable after some common transformations, but extensive alterations can prevent detection.
claims.source_title: Verify AI-generated images, videos and audio

claims.claim: Google previously described SynthID Detector as a portal that can highlight portions of media more likely to contain a watermark, including specific audio segments and image areas.
claims.source_title: SynthID Detector: Identify content made with Google’s AI tools

metadata.description:
Google’s SynthID Detector lets you upload an image, video, or audio file and check for an invisible watermark linked to AI-generated or AI-edited content. A detected mark may highlight part of the file and can involve Google or partner systems such as OpenAI, NVIDIA, or Kakao.

But SynthID is a clue, not a final verdict. A positive result does not explain every second of a file, while “not detected” does not prove something was made by a person. Here’s how to use the check before sharing dramatic clips online.
